blocks.text: These, then, are roughly the interpretations of the word שפן saphan given by the ancients. Which of them one should choose is not yet clear, for there is none of them that does not have its own difficulties. الوبر [al-wabr] alvvebro, that is, the mountain mouse, differs from the שפן saphan in that it does not ruminate, does not live among rocks, and is not native to Judaea or to the neighbouring regions ^{(5)}. That Pliny is objected against this to no purpose will be shown below. There is more reason on the side of those who hold that the saphan is الغنك [al-ghnk] alphenec, a species of squirrel, which the ancients called the Pontic mouse. For Pontic mice do ruminate. Aristotle, near the end of book 9 of the History [col. 1009] [II, 419] of Animals: Μηρυκάζουσι δὲ καὶ τῶν ἀμφοδόντων ἔνια, οἷον οἱ μῦες οἱ Ποντικοί [Mērykazousi de kai tōn amphodontōn enia, hoion hoi myes hoi Pontikoi]. There are also some among the animals with teeth in both jaws that ruminate, such as the Pontic mice. Pliny, book 10, chapter 73: Pontic mice also chew the cud in a similar way. And although they are mostly born in cold places, they are not lacking in hot ones either. Writers, indeed, mention a Gaetulian squirrel, and John Caius the Englishman has a good deal about it in his Letter to Gesner. I pass over the Arabian Geographer ^{a)}, who, in his list of the animals nourished by the forests of the Negroes in the interior of Africa, also includes افناك [afnāk], Finnic or Pontic mice. They do not, however, live among rocks; rather, they build their nests and rear their young at the tops of trees. Therefore الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec, or the Finnic mouse, cannot be the שפן saphan. The same judgement applies to the hyaena, which does not ruminate and does not live among rocks, but rather in tombs. Hence the den of a hyaena is called in Arabic رجمة [rujma] rugma, that is, a tomb. Moreover, Solomon says that the שפנים sephanim are a feeble folk, Prov. XXX, 26, which no one would say of hyaenas. Nor is the hedgehog among the ruminants, nor does it live among rocks, but in hollow trees, or in thickets or hedges. Hence the English call the hedgehog Hedge-hog, as if one were to say pig of the hedges. Nor should what I am about to say be lightly passed over. The marmot and the hyaena are solitary animals; so too is the hedgehog, which in Greek is called χὴρ [chēr] ἀπὸ τῆς χηρώσεως, ἤτοι ἐρημώσεως [apo tēs chērōseōs, ētoi erēmōseōs], from solitude. But the שפן saphan is a gregarious animal. To this belongs the fact that Solomon, in the place cited above, calls the שפנים sephanim a people: שפנים עם לא עצום, The Sephanim are a feeble people; just as a little earlier he says of the ants, הנמלים עם לא עז, The ants are a people not strong. And Joel. I, 6. of the locusts: גוי עלה על ארצי עצום, A strong nation has come up against my land. Of the same kind is what Lucian said in the Icaromenippus, μυρμήκων ἀγορὰν [myrmēkōn agoran], an assembly of ants. And Philip in the Anthology, book 1, chapter 23: Βωλοτόμοι μύρμηκες, ὁ γῆς στρατός [Bōlotomoi myrmēkes, ho gēs stratos]; Clod-hollowing ants, the army of the earth. And Philostratus says πιθήκων δῆμος [pithēkōn dēmos], as Solinus says the commons of the apes; and Smyrnaeus says μελισσάων κλυτὰ φῦλα [melissaōn klyta phyla], the noble nations of bees; and long before them the supreme Poet, Iliad 2:
Ἠΰτε ἔθνεα εἶσι μελισσάων ἀδινάων, [Ēyte ethnea eisi melissaōn adinaōn,]

as the nations of thronging bees go forth, that is, swarms. Of this phrase more elsewhere. Therefore, whatever the שפן saphan may be, it is not a solitary animal. And either the saphan is not the χοιρογρύλλιος [choirogryllios], as the most ancient translators rendered it, or the χοιρογρύλλιος [choirogryllios] is not the ἐχῖνος [echinos], the hedgehog, as they hold. And indeed the same Jerome who, in Psalm 104, carried away by the torrent of the other translators, renders it hedgehog, expressly teaches in his Letter to Sunia that the χοιρογρύλλιον [choirogryllion] is an animal different from the hedgehog, namely the ἀρκτομῦν [arktomyn]. His words are: It should be known that it is an animal not [II, 420] larger than a hedgehog, resembling a mouse and a bear. Hence in Palestine it is called ἀρκτομῦς [arktomys] [bear-mouse]. And there is a great abundance of this kind in those regions, and they are always accustomed to live in the caverns of rocks and in holes in the ground. And in the Coptic Lexicon ΠΙΧΙΡΟΓΡΙΛΛΙΟΝ, that is, ὁ χοιρογρύλλιος [ho choirogryllios], is rendered in Arabic اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. The crux of the question therefore turns on this: that we should know what the Greek ἀρκτομῦς [arktomys] and the Arabic اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] are. Nor should the reader find it tedious if I examine this more carefully, since we cannot otherwise come to know something hitherto unknown, namely what animal the Elders called χοιρογρύλλιον [choirogryllion] and the Hebrews שפן saphan.
